summary.text: For any bound, apply the assumed decomposition to \(n=(N+1)!/6\) with sufficiently large \(N\), writing \((N+1)!=(6x-1)+(6y+1)\), where \(6x-1\) is Sophie Germain and \(6y-1,6y+1\) are twin primes. If either relevant prime were at most \(N\), it would divide \((N+1)!\) and hence the other prime; primality would force them equal, giving \((N+1)!=2p\le 2N\), contrary to the factorial growth bound, so the construction yields arbitrarily large primes of both kinds.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\sum_{1\le x<n} I(x,n-x),
\]
where \(I(x,y)=1\) if all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime, and \(I(x,y)=0\) otherwise. Thus \(A(n)\) is the number of decompositions \(n=x+y\), with \(x,y>0\), for which \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime and \(6y-1,6y+1\) are twin primes. Indeed,
\[
2(6x-1)+1=12x-1.
\]

Assume throughout that
\[
A(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove separately that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

First record two elementary factorial facts.

**Factorial estimate.** If \(N\ge 7\), then
\[
(N+1)!>2N.
\]
One can prove this by induction on \(N\). At \(N=7\), it says \(8!=40320>14\). For the induction step, suppose \((N+1)!>2N\), where \(N\ge7\). Then
\[
2(N+1)<4N<2(N+1)!\le (N+2)(N+1)!=(N+2)!,
\]
so \((N+2)!>2(N+1)\), as required.

Also, if \(N\ge7\), then
\[
n:=\frac{(N+1)!}{6}>1.
\]
Indeed, \(N+1\ge8\), so \((N+1)!\ge8!=40320\), and hence its quotient by \(6\) is certainly greater than \(1\). Moreover, \(6\mid (N+1)!\), because \(6\le N+1\). Consequently
\[
6n=(N+1)!.
\]

We will repeatedly use the following consequence of the positivity of \(A(n)\). Since \(A(n)\) is a finite sum of terms each equal to either \(0\) or \(1\), if \(A(n)>0\), at least one term equals \(1\). Thus there are integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
1\le x<n,\qquad y=n-x,
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Since \(x<n\), we have \(y\ge1\), and \(x+y=n\).

We now prove the two infinitude statements.

## Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

It is enough to show that for every nonnegative integer \(a\), there is a Sophie Germain prime greater than \(a\).

Fix \(a\), and set
\[
N=\max(a,7),\qquad n=\frac{(N+1)!}{6}.
\]
Then \(N\ge7\), so \(n>1\). By the assumed positivity of \(A(n)\), choose \(x,y\ge1\) with
\[
x+y=n
\]
and with all four of
\[
6x-1,\quad12x-1,\quad6y-1,\quad6y+1
\]
prime.

Put
\[
p=6x-1.
\]
Then \(p\) is prime, and
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is also prime. Hence \(p\) is a Sophie Germain prime. We claim that \(p>a\).

Suppose to the contrary that \(p\le a\). Since \(a\le N\), this gives \(p\le N\). Also \(x\ge1\), so
\[
p=6x-1\ge5.
\]
In particular, \(1\le p\le N+1\), and therefore \(p\mid(N+1)!\), because every positive integer at most \(N+1\) occurs as a factor of \((N+1)!\).

On the other hand, from \(x+y=n\) and \(6n=(N+1)!\), we obtain
\[
(N+1)!=6x+6y=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+(6y+1).
\]
Thus
\[
6y+1=(N+1)!-p.
\]
Since \(p\) divides both \((N+1)!\) and itself, it divides their difference \(6y+1\).

But \(6y+1\) is prime. A positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself. Since \(p\ge5\), the possibility \(p=1\) is excluded. Therefore
\[
p=6y+1.
\]
It follows that
\[
(N+1)!=p+(6y+1)=2p.
\]
Because \(p\le N\), this yields
\[
(N+1)!=2p\le2N,
\]
contradicting the factorial estimate \((N+1)!>2N\).

Therefore \(p>a\). As \(a\) was arbitrary, Sophie Germain primes occur above every bound, and hence there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes.

## Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

Again, it suffices to show that for every nonnegative integer \(a\), some lower member of a twin-prime pair is greater than \(a\).

Fix \(a\), and now set
\[
N=\max(a+2,7),\qquad n=\frac{(N+1)!}{6}.
\]
Then \(N\ge7\), so \(n>1\). Positivity of \(A(n)\) supplies \(x,y\ge1\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad12x-1,\quad6y-1,\quad6y+1
\]
are prime.

Put
\[
r=6y-1.
\]
Both \(r\) and
\[
r+2=6y+1
\]
are prime, so \((r,r+2)\) is a twin-prime pair. We claim that \(r>a\).

Suppose instead that \(r\le a\). Let
\[
q=r+2=6y+1.
\]
Then
\[
q\le a+2\le N.
\]
Since \(y\ge1\), we also have \(q=6y+1\ge7\). Thus \(1\le q\le N+1\), and consequently
\[
q\mid(N+1)!.
\]

The identity \(x+y=n\), together with \(6n=(N+1)!\), gives
\[
(N+1)!=6x+6y=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=(6x-1)+q.
\]
Hence
\[
6x-1=(N+1)!-q.
\]
Because \(q\) divides both \((N+1)!\) and itself, it follows that
\[
q\mid 6x-1.
\]
The number \(6x-1\) is prime. Therefore its positive divisor \(q\) is either \(1\) or \(6x-1\). The first option is impossible because \(q\ge7\), so
\[
q=6x-1.
\]
It follows that
\[
(N+1)!=(6x-1)+q=2q.
\]
But \(q\le N\), so this implies
\[
(N+1)!=2q\le2N,
\]
again contradicting \((N+1)!>2N\).

Thus \(r>a\). Since \(a\) was arbitrary, lower members of twin-prime pairs occur above every bound. Hence there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

We have proved that the assumption \(A(n)>0\) for every \(n>1\) implies both that the set of Sophie Germain primes is infinite and that the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs is infinite, which is the desired conclusion.
